notes: Ruling slot 4 = National Liberation Front (National Front) after the Corrective Move of 22 June 1969; the state is still the People's Republic of Southern Yemen until 30 Nov 1970. Salimin's Maoist-leaning wing in 19, Radfan guerrilla veterans in 5, orthodox pro-Soviet PDU as hardliners in 6, security apparatus in 7, ousted Qahtan al-Shaabi loyalists in 13. Exile opposition: South Arabian League (MD's League of Yemen's Sons) in 1, FLOSY in 18, ATUC in 3, Beihan exiles in 0, Qu'aiti dynasty in 23.

0.name: Rijal Bayhan
0.text:
The exiles of Beihan, the frontier emirate whose Sharif Husayn bin Ahmad al-Habili was the strongest of the federal princes and Britain's closest ally in South Arabia. Since independence he and his tribesmen have operated from Saudi territory and the border of the Yemen Arab Republic, raiding into the South with Saudi money and arms.

They aim to overthrow the National Front by force, restore the princes and shaikhs of the former Federation of South Arabia and bring the South back into the Western and Saudi orbit. Authoritarian, anti-communist and tribal, their leverage lies in Saudi patronage and the guns of the frontier tribes.

1.name: Rabitat Abna' al-Janub al-Arabi
1.text:
The oldest nationalist organisation of the South, founded in Aden in 1951 by Muhammad Ali al-Jifri with the support of Lahej and Hadrami notables. It campaigned for an independent South Arabian state free of both British rule and absorption into Yemen, but lost the struggle for power to the National Front and is now banned, its leaders in exile in Saudi Arabia and Cairo.

The League stands for a conservative, Islamic and market-friendly South Arabian state, respect for property and tradition, and partnership with Saudi Arabia and the West. Fiercely anti-communist, it keeps followers among merchants, Hadramis and exiles; Saudi backing is its main leverage.

2.name: Muthaqqafu Adan
2.text:
The lawyers, clerks, teachers, doctors and journalists of Crater, Tawahi and Ma'alla, educated in the colony's English and Arabic schools and heirs to the constitutionalism of the Aden Association and the press of Muhammad Ali Luqman. Since independence many have lost their posts or left for Taizz, Cairo and the Gulf, while those who stay keep their heads down.

They want the rule of law, a free press, an independent judiciary, elected councils and the protection of private property and professional life against the National Front's committees. Open to the West and the Arab world alike, their leverage lies in skills the new state cannot replace.

3.name: Al-Mu'tamar al-Ummali
3.text:
The federation of Aden's port, refinery and service unions founded in 1956, once the strongest labour movement in the Arabian Peninsula and the backbone of the anti-colonial strikes. Its leader Abdullah al-Asnaj took it into FLOSY, and since the National Front's victory its independent leadership has been dissolved, its officials replaced by Front loyalists and many exiled to Taizz.

Its surviving members stand for free trade unions, collective bargaining, and wages and welfare won by organised labour rather than decreed by a party, and look to the Arab and international free union movement rather than the Soviet model. Their leverage lies in the dockers and refinery workers who can still paralyse Aden.

4.name: Al-Jabha al-Qawmiyya
4.native_full: Al-Jabha al-Qawmiyya li-Tahrir al-Janub al-Yamani al-Muhtall
4.text:
The ruling party of the People's Republic of Southern Yemen, founded in 1963 from the Arab Nationalist Movement's southern branch and tribal fighters, which launched the Radfan uprising and won independence from Britain in November 1967. The Corrective Move of 22 June 1969 removed President Qahtan al-Shaabi and gave power to the left: Salim Rubai Ali chairs the Presidential Council, Abdul Fattah Ismail runs the party apparatus and Muhammad Ali Haitham is prime minister.

The Front proclaims scientific socialism: nationalisation of banks, trade and insurance, land reform, mass organisations, a people's militia and a vanguard party. Aligned with the Soviet Union and China, it backs the Dhofar revolution and controls state, army and unions.

5.name: Fida'iyyu Radfan
5.text:
The veteran guerrillas of the mountain war that began in Radfan on 14 October 1963, tribesmen and young militants who fought the British in the hills and in Aden's streets and now form the armed core of the National Front. Commanders such as Ali Antar keep their prestige and their weapons, and resent the old British-trained officers and the cautious bureaucrats.

They want the revolution carried further and faster: popular militias in place of the regular army, land and boats seized by peasants and fishermen, and armed support for the revolutions in Dhofar and the North. Impatient with diplomacy, their leverage lies in arms, their standing as liberators and their hold on the rural districts.

6.name: Ittihad al-Sha'b al-Dimuqrati
6.text:
Yemen's first Marxist-Leninist party, founded in Aden in 1961 by Abdullah Abd al-Razzaq Badhib, the teacher and journalist who introduced Soviet-style Marxism to South Arabia. Small and intellectual, it stood apart from the armed struggle, but since the Corrective Move of 1969 it has drawn close to the National Front's left, and Badhib serves in the government.

It defends Marxist-Leninist orthodoxy against the Front's Maoist and adventurist tendencies: a disciplined vanguard, central planning, a strong state and unconditional alignment with the Soviet Union and its allies. Its leverage lies in theory, cadres trained in Moscow and East Berlin, and its patrons' embassy channels.

7.name: Ayn al-Thawra
7.text:
The security apparatus the National Front has built since independence from its own intelligence cadres, inheriting the colonial Special Branch files and seeking instructors from East Germany and the Soviet Union. It runs the political police, the prisons and the hunt for the sultans' agents, Saudi-backed infiltrators and suspected rightists.

Its officers believe the revolution survives only through vigilance: arrests without trial, purges of the army and administration, control of travel and the press, and an alliance with the socialist camp against imperialism and Saudi reaction. Answerable to the Front's leadership but feared by it, its leverage lies in files, prisons and fear.

8.name: Jama'at al-Buhra
8.text:
The Ismaili Shia trading community of Aden, of Gujarati origin, gathered around its mosques and community halls and owing allegiance to the Dai al-Mutlaq in Bombay, Syedna Mohammed Burhanuddin. Merchants, shopkeepers and craftsmen, many families have left since independence and the nationalisations of 1969, but a core remains.

Apolitical by doctrine, the community seeks only the freedom to worship, run its schools and trusts, and trade, and offers loyalty to whatever government guarantees these. Neither Western nor Eastern in orientation, its leverage lies in commercial skills, overseas connections and its usefulness as an intermediary with India and East Africa.

9.name: Ahl al-Najaf
9.text:
A few Twelver Shia families of Aden, Khojas of Indian origin and Persian merchants, whose sons study in or correspond with the seminaries of Najaf, where the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini is lecturing this winter on government by the Islamic jurist. Their numbers are shrinking as the foreign merchant communities leave Aden.

The young among them reject both the quietism of their elders and the National Front's atheism, and hold that only an order guided by the clergy can resist imperialism and godless Marxism alike. Isolated and watched by the security services, their leverage lies only in religious conviction and ties to Najaf.

10.name: Sadat Tarim
10.text:
The Ba Alawi sayyids of Tarim and the Hadramawt valley, descendants of the Prophet whose Sufi scholarship, religious colleges such as the Ribat of Tarim and networks reaching Java, East Africa and the Hijaz have defined Hadrami Islam for centuries. Scholars such as Muhammad bin Salim bin Hafiz keep teaching in Tarim under growing pressure from the National Front's campaign against religion and privilege.

They stand for established Sunni orthodoxy, sharia courts, pious endowments, social hierarchy and loyalty to legitimate rulers, and look to Saudi Arabia and the Hadrami diaspora for protection. Their leverage lies in religious prestige, endowments and the devotion of the Hadrami faithful at home and abroad.

11.name: Ansar al-Khilafa
11.text:
A clandestine circle of young Adenis and Hadramis, students and clerks shaped by the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir and the writings of Sayyid Qutb, which reach them through Kuwait, Jordan and the Hadrami diaspora. Appalled by the National Front's attacks on religion, they meet secretly in mosques and homes and pass on banned literature.

They hold that nationalism and Marxism alike are idolatry and that only a restored caliphate ruling by God's law can save the Muslims, rejecting both superpowers and every existing Arab government. Without arms or patrons, their leverage lies in religious outrage at the regime's secularism.

12.name: Jam'iyyat al-Islah wa-l-Irshad
12.text:
The reformist association founded in Batavia in 1914 by the Sudanese scholar Ahmad Surkati among Hadrami emigrants in the Dutch East Indies, which challenged the hereditary privileges of the sayyids and preached a modern, scripture-based Islam. Its ideas returned home with emigrants and shaped a generation of non-sayyid Hadrami merchants, teachers and reformers.

Its followers advocate Islamic renewal through education, equality among believers, modern schools and charitable works, and reject both sayyid hierarchy and atheistic Marxism. Moderate and mercantile, linked to Indonesia, Singapore and Saudi Arabia, their leverage lies in schools, money and the Hadrami diaspora.

13.name: Ansar Qahtan
13.text:
The followers of Qahtan Muhammad al-Shaabi, the National Front's first leader and the republic's first president, deposed by the Corrective Move of 22 June 1969 and now held under house arrest in Aden. Faisal Abd al-Latif al-Shaabi, his former prime minister, sits in prison, and their partisans have been purged from the party and administration.

They stand for a pragmatic nationalist one-party state: independence first, cautious economic change, a professional army and civil service, good relations with Cairo and the Arab states, and neutrality between East and West. Silenced but not extinct, their leverage lies in former officials, officers and Arab nationalist sympathies.

14.name: Wujaha' Hadramawt
14.text:
The merchants, landowners, tribal chiefs and religious families of the Hadramawt, the vast eastern region once divided between the Qu'aiti and Kathiri sultanates and joined to the new republic in 1967. Proud of its distinct history and its emigrant wealth, the Hadramawt has seen its sultans exiled and its administration in Mukalla replaced by National Front committees.

The notables want regional autonomy, respect for property, religion and tribal custom, and an administration run by Hadramis rather than socialist experiments decreed from Aden. Neutral between the blocs, their leverage lies in the remittances and goodwill of the Hadrami diaspora and the region's sheer size.

15.name: Buyut Jidda al-Hadramiyya
15.text:
The great Hadrami merchant and banking families who made their fortunes in Saudi Arabia, led by Salim bin Mahfouz, founder of the National Commercial Bank, and builders and traders such as the Bugshan family. Their capital, contracts and charity have long sustained the towns of Wadi Hadramawt and Wadi Du'an.

They regard the National Front's nationalisations of November 1969 as theft and its socialism as a threat to their families, lands and endowments at home. Pro-Saudi and pro-Western, they fund the exile opposition and wait for a government that will respect property; their leverage lies in money and access to the Saudi court.

16.name: Ahl al-Mina' al-Hurr
16.text:
The shipping agents, bunkering firms, duty-free shopkeepers and traders of Aden's Steamer Point, whose free port was once among the busiest in the world. The closure of the Suez Canal in June 1967, the British withdrawal and the nationalisations of 1969 have emptied the harbour and sent many of them to Djibouti, Dubai and Jeddah.

They want Aden restored as a free port and entrepot: no customs duties, a convertible currency, private shipping and banking, and open doors to every flag regardless of ideology. Indifferent to the Cold War but hostile to central planning, their leverage lies in the port economy on which Aden's survival depends.

17.name: Ahl Suqutra
17.text:
The herders, fishermen and date growers of Socotra, an isolated island in the Arabian Sea, formerly ruled by the Mahri sultan of Qishn and Socotra and now administered from Aden. Speaking their own language, they live among dragon's blood and frankincense trees found nowhere else, managing grazing and water by ancient customary rules.

They seek to be left alone: protection of grazing land, trees and fishing grounds from outsiders, respect for island custom, and supplies and medicine in return for loyalty. Untouched by the Cold War except for foreign interest in the island's strategic position, their leverage lies only in remoteness.

18.name: Jabhat Tahrir Janub al-Yaman al-Muhtall
18.english: Front for the Liberation of Occupied South Yemen
18.text:
The Nasserist front formed in January 1966 by Abdullah al-Asnaj's People's Socialist Party and former Aden chief minister Abdul Qawi Makkawi, with Egyptian backing. It fought the British and then the National Front in a bitter civil war that it lost in 1967, and its leaders and fighters now live in exile in Cairo and the Yemen Arab Republic.

FLOSY stands for Arab socialism on the Egyptian model, Yemeni unity, trade-union rights and a plural nationalist movement in place of the National Front's Marxist dictatorship. Backed by Cairo and tolerated by Sana'a, its leverage lies in exile networks, Adeni workers and Egyptian goodwill.
18.wiki: Front for the Liberation of Occupied South Yemen

19.name: Rifaq Salimin
19.text:
The Maoist-inclined wing of the National Front gathered around Salim Rubai Ali, known as Salimin, chairman of the Presidential Council and a former guerrilla leader from Abyan. Inspired by China's Cultural Revolution and impatient with bureaucracy, it draws on militiamen, rural cadres and youth, and welcomes growing Chinese aid and advice.

It calls for a revolution from below: peasants and fishermen seizing land and boats, mass campaigns against officials and the bourgeoisie, an armed people in place of the regular army, austerity and self-reliance. Wary of becoming a Soviet client, it keeps Peking close; its leverage lies in Salimin's popularity and the countryside.

20.name: Qaba'il al-Awaliq
20.text:
The tribes of the Upper and Lower Awlaqi country in Shabwa, whose sons formed the backbone of the British-trained Federal Army and its officer corps. After the army's move against the National Front's left in March 1968 and the purges that followed, many Awlaqi officers and shaikhs have been arrested, retired or driven into exile.

Their grievance has become a southern nativism: resentment of Front leaders born in the North, of the militia and of Aden's committees, and a demand that the army and the land remain in the hands of the South's own tribes. Courted by Saudi Arabia and the exiles, their leverage lies in arms and the soldiers still in uniform.

21.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki
21.text:
The Aden branch of the pan-Arab Ba'ath, organised since the late 1950s among teachers, students and civil servants, which took part in the anti-colonial struggle outside the National Front. Its leading figures, among them Anis Hasan Yahya, keep a small, disciplined organisation that cooperates with the regime while guarding its own identity.

It stands for Arab unity, freedom and socialism under a vanguard party, a militarised society and a single Arab nation, and argues that the South's revolution must serve the whole Arab nation rather than Marxist internationalism. Its leverage lies in its intellectuals and its ties to Baghdad and Damascus.

22.name: Al-Quwwat al-Musallaha
22.native_full: Al-Quwwat al-Musallaha li-Jumhuriyyat al-Yaman al-Janubiyya al-Sha'biyya
22.text:
The armed forces inherited from the British-trained Federal Regular Army and Federal Guard, renamed and purged since independence. After the officers' move against the National Front's left in March 1968, the Front has dismissed hundreds of tribal officers, introduced political instructors and placed the army under Defence Minister Ali Nasir Muhammad.

The professional officers who remain value order, hierarchy and the army's autonomy and distrust the militias and the ideologues, even as Soviet arms and advisers begin to arrive. Their leverage lies in being the only conventional force facing Saudi-backed raids and the frontier with the North.

23.name: Al al-Qu'ayti
23.text:
The dynasty of Yafa'i origin that ruled the Qu'aiti Sultanate of Shihr and Mukalla, the largest and richest state of the Hadramawt, under British protection until its collapse in September 1967. Its young Sultan Ghalib bin Awadh al-Qu'aiti, educated in Britain, lives in exile in Saudi Arabia, where many of the deposed rulers of the South have gathered.

The Qu'aitis and their fellow exiled rulers seek the restoration of the sultanates, the return of confiscated property and a Hadramawt separate from Aden's revolution. Pro-Saudi and pro-Western, their leverage lies in Hadrami merchant wealth, Saudi protection and the memory of an orderly, modernising Mukalla.
